units.translation: 813a. Naiads tend him: he means Chariclo and Philyra, by whom Achilles was raised; of these Chariclo was the wife of Chiron, and Philyra his mother.

814-15a. Need of the maiden: Anaxagoras says that in truth the inhabitants of Laconia honored Achilles as a god; but some say that the gods, sympathizing with Thetis, made him immortal. That Achilles went to the Elysian plain and married Medea was first stated by Ibycus (fg 37 B. III 248), after him Simonides (fg 213 B. III 527).

816. And to Peleus himself: the author of the Aegimius in the second book (Hesiod fr. 185 Rz.²) says that Thetis threw the children born from Peleus into a cauldron of water, wishing to know if they were mortal, but others say into fire, as Apollonius (IV 869 ff.) says; and indeed when many had been destroyed, Peleus became angry and prevented Achilles from being thrown into the cauldron. Sophocles in the Lovers of Achilles (fr. 151 Pearson) says that Thetis, having been reviled by Peleus, left him. Staphylus in the third book of his Thessalian Affairs (fr. 2 M. IV 505) says that Chiron, being wise and experienced in astronomy, wishing to make Peleus famous,

sent for 〈Philomela〉 the daughter of Actor the Myrmidon and spread reports that Peleus was about to marry Thetis, Zeus giving her to him, and that the gods would come with rain and storm. Having spread this rumor, he watched for a time when there were heavy rains and violent winds, and gave Philomela to Peleus; and thus the report prevailed.
820. Blasts of winds: the turnings to either side in war; but Apollonius has spoken of the contrary blasts of the winds.

825-31a. Do not you either Charybdis: Sicily lies opposite Italy, and between them is a strait of two hundred stades 〈...〉 from Sicily to Italy. 〈...〉 So the one promontory, Pelorus, looks toward Italy, below which is the so-called Charybdis, while Scylla is again in Italy opposite Pelorus. This Scylla is a headland jutting out into the sea, having the likeness and face of a woman. Below the headland are very many large rocks, having hollow places and caves, in which sea monsters dwell, which, when ships are driven there against the rocks 〈...〉.
